20	BY MR. TREVISANI:


Q: Good morning, Dr. Paulson.
A: Good morning.

Q: Could you tell us where you are right now?
A: I'm in Salem, Oregon.

Q: And where in Salem?
A: South Hills.

Q: Oh. I don't need the address, but are you in your house, in your office?
A: I'm in my home, yes.

Q: Okay. Is there anybody there in the room with you?
A: No.

Q: Okay. I'm going to go over a couple of basics for the deposition. One is, especially with the Zoom, you have to make sure to respond orally so that the court reporter can take it down. Make sure to wait until I finish the question before you answer so we don't talk over each other. And if you don't understand any of the questions, just let me know. I will try to rephrase it. But if you don't say anything, I'm going to assume that you understood the question. Is that okay?
A: Yes.

Q: Okay. Did you bring -- do you have any documents in -- with you there in the room that you intend to refer to during the deposition?
A: Nothing that I intend to refer to.

Q: Great. Do you have a copy of your declaration?
A: Yes. That, I have right here.

Q: Okay. Do you have any other documents that you relied on for your opinion available to you on the computer?
A: Not easily so.

Q: Okay. So other than your declaration, do you have any other documents there with you?
A: I have -- this was not in my declaration, though. I have a report from the recordations concerning the use of restrictive housing from the Department of Justice, 2016.

Q: Okay. Anything else?
A: That's it.

Q: Okay. MR. TREVISANI: Merinda, could we bring up Exhibit DHA01210933, which should be Dr. Paulson's CV. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This will be Exhibit 1, Paulson 1. MR. TREVISANI: Yes. Thank you. (Exhibit 1 marked.) THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: It's there on the screen. Would you like control? MR. TREVISANI: Yes, please. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: You have control. (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Dr. Paulson, I'm going to scroll through here. I'm going to make it a little bit bigger here for you.
A: Okay.

Q: If I can figure out how to do that.
A: Is this a second window I can move?

Q: I don't think you have control here, but --
A: Okay.

Q: -- I can give it to you, if you need to. But let me just scroll through it here.
A: All right.

Q: And, unfortunately, all the page numbers seem to be 2, but the last Bates number is DHA01210945. Is this your current CV, Dr. Paulson?
A: What I could see looks like it, yes.

Q: Okay. I want to ask you a couple of questions about your background. You received a master's in public health in 1990; is that right?
A: Yes.

Q: Did any of that training for your master's in public health involve any correctional medicine training?
A: Not directly so.

Q: Okay. How about indirectly?
A: I -- the -- my focus for that was in program planning.

Q: Okay. What's program planning?
A: It's, essentially, the -- like it sounds. It's putting together and writing programs for medical circumstances.

Q: Okay. And then here, it says you received a master's training in research 1978-1980.
A: Yes.

Q: What is that degree?
A: That was in neurophysiology.

Q: And then, going down to your residency, did your residency have any particular specialty?
A: Family medicine.

Q: And did that involve any training or experience with correctional medicine?
A: To some extent. A lot of it was emergency room. Also, the County of Los Angeles had both a sheriff's office and -- it was a hospital of choice for hospitalizations regarding inmates for that portion of Los Angeles.

Q: But you treated those people in a hospital, right?
A: In hospital, yes.

Q: You didn't treat them in the jail?
A: No.

Q: Okay. And then scrolling down on your CV, to -- in 2019, it says, "Certified Correctional Health Care Provider - Physician," from the "National Commission on Correctional Health Care." Can you tell me about that certification?
A: That certification involves two -- two prerequisite certifications and is about essentially being familiar with and reasons for the various standards that the NCCHC holds for jails and prisons.

Q: So what do you have to do to become eligible for the certification?
A: Study and -- and take an exam.

Q: Is there any experience requirement?
A: Let me think. I don't recall.

Q: Have you published any papers in any peer-reviewed journals?
A: No.

Q: Have you conducted any research in correctional medicine?
A: Not other than in -- in quality assurance in my position as chief medical officer of the Oregon State Penitentiary.

Q: Okay. And so you haven't also conducted any research in health care provided in solitary confinement?
A: Not published, no.

Q: Okay. And same question. You haven't conducted any research on health care provided to people in restrictive housing?
A: Not published, no.

Q: And is there unpublished research?
A: Well, like I said, doing the quality assurance and monitoring in our own system.

Q: So it looks like you started with the Oregon Department of Corrections in 2009. Is that right?
A: That sounds right.

Q: All right. I'm looking for the -- ah, give me a second. There we go. Okay. So why did you take that job?
A: Number of reasons. I'd been working emergency most of my career. And I was in my mid 50s, and the nights were killing me. That was probably the biggest one. I had a young family, and I was missing recitals and things, because it's a 24/7 matter. So I was looking for, primarily, something that didn't have night and weekend work. I knew two physicians who had worked for the department. One ran -- that I worked with as a colleague in the same clinic for a number of years, and another that I graduated from medical school with. Both had worked, and one of them was continuing to work, with the Oregon Department of Corrections.

Q: So your current job is chief medical officer for the Oregon State Penitentiary; is that right?
A: Yes, but I'm in transition.

Q: And what's the transition?
A: I'm transitioning to retiring. So I'm not seeing patients directly in clinic at this point. I'm consulting on lots of cases. And they haven't replaced me as chief medical officer yet. But when they do, I'll stop those duties.

Q: Okay. So I want to talk to you --
A: (Inaudible) sometime next year.

Q: Understood. So I want to talk about your job throughout your time at the Oregon State Penitentiary. Have you had the same job from 2009 to the present?
A: I've -- I've -- the position of the correctional medi- -- pardon me -- correctional physician specialist in the department gives us ability to move from -- from site to site. So my job has been the same, but I have had different sites.

Q: So in this whole time, were you the chief medical officer for the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: No.

Q: Okay. So what years were you the chief medical officer for the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: That, I always have to think a bit about. It's been, I think, the last six, almost seven, years.

Q: So when you came to the Oregon Department of Corrections in 2009, what was your job?
A: My job was to be a physician on -- on staff there.

Q: Okay. So -- and then, did you have any other jobs before you transitioned to becoming the chief medical officer of the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: Well, within my duties there, I was a physician in charge of direct care to the segregated housing units and mental health infirmary, Death Row, behavioral health unit. I continued that for a while when I was the chief medical officer. Also, I had the same, similar duties at Coffee Creek, what would be on your -- you covered multiple places, but -- and I can't remember. It's probably -- I was chief medical officer for a year or so when we finally got another staff member and I was able to -- to hand over the segregation and mental health unit's medical care.

Q: So what years were you responsible for the medical care in the segregation units and the mental health care?
A: That, again, I have to think. Because for two years, I was working -- I was covering both Coffee Creek, which is the intake center and women's prisons, and OSP. And somewhere in that two-year period, I was transitioning from one to the other and was able to take up the duties. So that would have been around 2012 or '13, I think. No. '13, '14. Again, it's just a guess.

Q: Okay. And then, I think you said that you became chief medical officer of the Oregon State Penitentiary roughly six or seven years ago?
A: Yes.

Q: So does 2015 sound about right?
A: 2014, 2015, something like that. It's when Dr. Degner retired. Again, since my position doesn't change, I don't have -- you don't apply for these -- these changes. Our -- our credentialing, essentially, is continuous through them. It's just what I'm doing on a particular day. And like I said, it -- there isn't a new job description, essentially, that comes from our -- my -- my position has been the same position with the department the whole time.

Q: And that position is correctional physician specialist?
A: Yeah, correctional physician specialist.

Q: So during the time that you were the chief medical officer, what were your duties and responsibilities?
A: It's -- it's largely about working to get the best medical care possible. I work with the physicians and nurse practitioners, PAs when we have them, as a -- as a resource. Essentially, it's like being a lead worker. I've got the most experience, both in practice and in the department. And on top of that, the -- there's a certain amount of QA that's done and a certain amount of -- of review of records that -- where there's a problem, and a certain amount of oversight for the mental health section, particularly in the area of involuntary medication.

Q: QA is quality assurance?
A: Yes.

Q: Is it fair to say that you're responsible for all the medical care provided at the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: No.

Q: Is there a person who is responsible for that?
A: We have licensed medical professionals being responsible for themselves.

Q: So does the chief medical officer -- are you the highest-ranking medical person at Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: It's not a ranking. Like I said, I'm essentially lead worker, there to give people help, to -- to make things better. I don't hire or fire anyone. I don't write anyone's performance review. The department has a medical director, but that's not me. And it's a really good thing, because that way, I'm not a threat to anybody. I'm just helping them do better medicine for our patients.

Q: Does anybody report to you?
A: Not report in the sense that -- that their job is -- that I'm responsible for their job. No. Like I said, I don't write anyone's performance reviews.

Q: Who do you report to?
A: To -- to the medical director.

Q: And is the medical director somebody who's at the Oregon State Penitentiary, or are they medical director for the entire Oregon Department of Corrections?
A: The director is over all the facilities.

Q: The entire Department of Corrections?
A: Yes.

Q: Do you have any responsibility for setting medical policy at Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: The policies and procedures, I've had input in that over the years. I've written several. And so in that regard, it's kind of a -- we're a small department, so everyone has a say. And like I said, I've -- I've been a writer on several of them in the past. I haven't done any lately.

Q: Okay. What percentage of your job now is treating patients?
A: I don't see patients directly at all right now.

Q: Okay. When did you stop seeing patients?
A: September.

Q: And so before September, what percentage of your job was treating patients?
A: Oh. Well, 100 percent, essentially, since I've never had carved-out, formal time for the chief medical officer work.

Q: Okay. So do you have any administrative responsibilities as the chief medical officer?
A: A certain amount of quality assurance and overseeing cases where there's -- there's a question of care, something like that. I'm generally the first person to look at that and -- within our -- our facility.

Q: What does the quality assurance look like?
A: The -- a quality assurance committee for health services in OSP. I'm the physician sitting on that -- that small committee. We do reviews of areas, some of them rotating and some of them permanent, essentially charted use of cases. The rotating ones are generally random. The permanent ones, like I -- I review -- review every death, every hospitalization where I can't get the record before the patient is transferred. And a certain amount of the emergency transfers, medical emergency transfers.

Q: Are there any regular audits of the medical care provided at Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: Like I said, there -- there's rotating quality assurance audits. And the department and OSP are part of the NCCHC, and they audit periodically.

Q: Okay. And the internal audits, are they conducted by Oregon Department of Corrections staff?
A: Yes. Well, there's the quality assurance audits we're talking about, yeah.

Q: Have you worked in any other correctional setting, other than the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: Just what's listed in my CV and my introduction declaration.

Q: Do you have any expertise in prison administration outside of the medical context?
A: No.

Q: What about, do you have any expertise in running a solitary confinement unit?
A: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the last part.

Q: Do you have any expertise in running a solitary confinement unit? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: Only in the medi- -- provision of medical care.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Going down to the page on your CV -- or, I guess, up, rather, there is a list here of various cases. And it looks like -- it looks like there are 10 cases listed there. Are those cases where you've served as an expert witnesses?
A: Yes.

Q: Are there any other than the ones that are listed here?
A: Is the last one -- is Harvard in there?

Q: Do you mean this case --
A: Yes.

Q: -- that we're on right now? Well, other than this case that we're on taking this deposition.
A: That needs to be added. And I'm just taking on another case right now that I'll work on after the first of the year.

Q: Okay. So other than that one and the Harvard case, there's none other than these that are listed here?
A: Correct.

Q: And then, it looks like, under correctional medical expert file depository experience here, there's this Hamblin case. And then it looks like the case is listed again in the second section here, Hamblin. Is that the same case?
A: Yes.

Q: And in any of these cases, did you give a deposition?
A: Well, in the Hamblin case.

Q: (Inaudible) other?
A: (No response.)

Q: Are there any other cases where you gave a deposition?
A: Yes. They're listed in my declaration.

Q: Okay. Can you tell me which ones?
A: Hamblin. Rojas versus Correct Care Solutions. The Estate of John Kleutsch versus State of Washington. Alejandro Gallegos versus K. Seeley. And, of course, this one right now.

Q: Okay. And did you testify at trial in any of those cases?
A: No.

Q: In the ones where you did not provide -- or you did not give a deposition, did you prepare an expert report?
A: Can you scroll down so I can see more?

Q: Sure.
A: It's easier to give you the exceptions. I have not given a report for Ramey or Carol Cole. The Carol Cole was a case that I dropped out of after reviewing. So that one, I didn't have any involvement past first review.

Q: Okay. Were -- were any of these -- in any of these cases, where you've been an expert, where you were retained by the plaintiff?
A: Yes. This list, Kleutsch, Thomsen, Widmayer. Can you roll on down. Rojas, Ramey, Perry, Hamblin and Ale- -- Gallegos.

Q: Okay. So was that all of them that -- where you were retained by the plaintiff?
A: All on this list, yes. I don't think this list is complete. This lists -- CV is -- could use some updating at this point.

Q: Oh. Well, that's why I asked you, are there any others that are listed here? I thought you told me there were not.
A: There's none that are -- there's none -- I'm sorry. I might have misunderstood you. These -- this list is somewhat old and doesn't include everything.

Q: Okay. So what are the other cases where you've been retained by an expert?
A: I would have to -- I would have to go to memory at this point, and I don't think I could give it accurately without looking through my records.

Q: Well, approximately how many are there, other than the ones --
A: It might be another two or three.

Q: Okay. So what percentage of the time, in all of the cases where you've been retained as an expert, were you retained by the plaintiff versus the defendant?
A: Oh, perhaps 75 or 80 percent.

Q: That was -- the 75, 80 percent was the plaintiff?
A: Were the plaintiffs, yes.

Q: Okay. These all -- these all -- the ones that are listed here -- well, I guess, let me ask it a different way. The cases where you've been retained as an expert, were they all involving one individual plaintiff seeking damages?
A: Yes.

Q: Okay. So have you ever been retained as an expert to do a case like you -- like you've been retained to do here in Harvard, where you evaluated a medical system?
A: Can you -- can you define what you mean there by "like"?

Q: Well, have you ever been retained as an expert where you've been asked to identi- -- to evaluate a system rather than just look at the care provided to one individual?
A: Well, a lot of cases involve looking at the system, but -- because, a lot of times, then, problems might arise from more than just a medical provider, such as transport or other administrative issues that are part of an individual case. But these -- these have all been individual cases with an -- where an individual inmate is part of the -- the question.

Q: That's what I'm asking. Are there any other cases where you're asking to evaluate a system, not for the care provided to one individual, but for the system as a whole?
A: No.

Q: So this Harvard case, this is the first time that you've done that? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: And let me -- let me extend that a little bit. I obviously help my department in that -- in cases of -- involving our department. And some of those have -- have been regarding the system. But, again, those -- this isn't the same thing as we've been talking about, being retained as an expert.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Any of the cases where you've been retained as an expert in the past, did the -- did those cases involve medical care that was being provided in solitary confinement or restrictive housing?
A: Yes.

Q: Which ones?
A: Well, let me look at this list. Thomsen, Widmayer. Can you roll -- scroll down? Ramey, Perry. That's it.

Q: Have you ever been excluded as an expert by a court?
A: No.

Q: Has the court -- has a court ever limited your testimony or your opinions?
A: No.

Q: Have you ever served as an expert for the Florida Department of Corrections before?
A: No.

Q: Have you ever been retained by the Rumberger Kirk law firm before?
A: No. MR. TREVISANI: If you could take down this exhibit.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) How did you first become involved with this case?
A: I believe I got an e-mail from one of the lawyers at Rumberger Kirk.

Q: Okay. And what were you asked to do for the case?
A: I was asked to review the medical care, and particularly regarding the complaint involved.

Q: Uh-huh. And what was your -- what was your assignment, so to speak?
A: Essentially, the area of allopathic medicine.

Q: Well, I mean, I guess I'm asking, what were you asked to do? What were you asked to give an opinion?
A: About the areas in the complaint, and -- and to review the medical care of the -- of the plaintiffs.

Q: Do you have some kind of retainer letter or engagement letter?
A: No. I think there are medical privacy letters, but I don't think there was a formal retainer letter.

Q: When were you retained?
A: Late winter. Mid-winter. Yeah. January, February, I believe.

Q: Of what year?
A: 2020 -- 2021.

Q: What did you do to prepare for today's deposition?
A: In -- in -- I've read through various pieces of information regarding the case, part -- things in the list. In particular, some of the plaintiffs' depositions and the particulars of my declaration, the Third Amended Complaint, and that's about it.

Q: Did you speak to anybody to prepare for the deposition?
A: No. MR. TREVISANI: Can we bring up an exhibit. It's called Dr. Reed Paulson Declaration. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This would be Paulson Exhibit 2. MR. TREVISANI: Yes. Thank you. (Exhibit 2 marked.) THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: It's on screen. Would you like control? MR. TREVISANI: Yes, please.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) I just wanted to be sure we're all looking at the same document. So let's see. This one is -- scroll down to the bottom. It's 55 pages long. Let's see. The actual declaration is Pages 1 through 45. And then on page 47 through the end is your CV. Is this the declaration that you submitted for this case?
A: It looks like it.

Q: Okay. MR. TREVISANI: We can go ahead and take that down. (BY MR. TREVISANI) I just wanted to make sure we have the exhibit, because I have a copy and I know you have a copy there, Dr. Paulson. Is that right, Dr. Paulson, you have a physical copy of it in front of you?
A: Yes.

Q: Okay. Tell me about the process for drafting your report, or your declaration. How did that go?
A: Well, it's a big case with -- with a lot of paperwork. Spent a lot of time going through the 40,000-plus pages of it. That's my guess about the 40,000, based on the thickness. A: Over a long period of time, yes. It's felt like -- it's felt that the benefit comes mostly from -- from easier blood pressure control. And so the benefit from blood pressure control comes over the course of years.

Q: So let's look at Jerome Burgess, Page 29 of your declaration. So your opinion is that -- well, let me ask you, is it your opinion that Mr. Burgess is having pseudoseizures?
A: That's the opinion of Dr. Gama and -- where's this other one -- Dr. Gaxiola.

Q: Do you agree with that opinion?
A: I have no reason to disagree with it. Those are his doctors, and one of them is his neurologist.

Q: And you agree or you believe that he has not have epilepsy?
A: I have no reason to disagree with his doctors.

Q: Well, is it your opinion that he pseudoseizures or epilepsy?
A: I don't have a medical opinion beyond the record I haven't examined him myself.

Q: Okay. So you don't have an opinion on what's causing Mr. Burgess's seizures? MS. SMITH: Objection; predicate.
A: I don't have a separate medical opinion about that. My observation is that his doctors say that they're pseudoseizures, both his neurologist and his general doctor. But that's going to be the case for any pretty much any inmate that we discuss. I need to depend on their physicians and such for a -- for a medical opinion of what's going on there for the most part.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) So for all of the individuals that you've reviewed, you don't have a medical opinion on their -- on their diseases? MS. SMITH: Overbroad.
A: I can't lend opinion beyond what's in the record. Now, such a thing as an X-ray that fails to show a fracture is an X-ray fails to a show a fracture. An X-ray that shows a fracture is an X-ray is shows that fracture. That's not too hard to work with. But I haven't seen the EEG that Mr. Burgess had. I saw an MRI report, I believe, and I have not seen him have an event so it's a little more difficult for him to -- for me to have a separate opinion than his doctors. I simply have no reason to doubt them.

Q: Okay. He's been prescribed seizure medications, right?
A: Yes.

Q: So there is at least a doctor who believes that he has epilepsy, right?
A: There was a provider that at one point wanted to cover him for epilepsy apparently or --

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Do you know --
A: -- and/or some of these medications are also used for mental health for mood stabilization or for chronic pain for pain control. So I don't know how he started on that or -- or from what all conditions that he's been continued on that, but it is a bit of an abundance of caution to have a seizure patient on that. It's not unusual.

Q: Is that within the standard of care to prescribe epilepsy medication to a patient who -- with pseudoseizures who has no evidence of epilepsy on an EEG? MS. SMITH: Overbroad; predicate.
A: It's certainly is -- is done, and like I said, these medications have multiple uses.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Do you know why they were prescribed for Mr. Burgess?
A: I don't know.

Q: So regardless of whether it's pseudoseizures or it's epilepsy, you would agree that he still faces the same risk of falling from a seizure, correct? MS. SMITH: Overbroad.
A: I don't know. The majority of the pseudoseizures patients fall carefully and don't bump themselves as often as those who have -- to epilepsy and have an event where they're at.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) So do you have an opinion on whether the risk faced to Mr. Burgess is the same or different depending upon whether he has pseudoseizures or epilepsy?
A: The risk of fall injury, I think, is less with pseudoseizures.

Q: Okay. At the top of Page 30 of your declaration, you say, "Mr. Burgess has refused to see neurology since then," and I think sometimes refers to 2015; is that right?
A: That I'm not sure.

Q: Well, you're not sure of which part?
A: Oh, yeah, I think I -- the 1/22/2015, okay, I see that, yeah. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. Can you bring up BUR 00004163. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This will be Exhibit 14. Share the screen. And you have control. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. So -- thank you. (Exhibit 14 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) This is Exhibits 14 is a neurology clinic flow sheet. Does that indicate that Burgess was seen in the neurology chronic care clinic in 5 of 2019?
A: I don't know. It -- he's receiving chronic care clinic visit, but we in primary care see our seizure disorder patients regularly in clinic without being neurologists. So we -- we have a chronic care form a little different than this, but my filling out that form doesn't make me a neurologist.

Q: But he is not -- Mr. Burgess is seen for neurologic care, correct?
A: He's seen in the -- in the -- in a seizure disorder chronic illness clinic, but we also see our pseudoseizure patients there. It depends --

Q: So even --
A: -- or where you do that documentation. So I can't say for sure.

Q: All I'm asking you is, in this clinic, he is receiving neurologic care, correct?
A: I can't -- if you allow me to include pseudoseizure, yes.

Q: Okay. So he did not refuse neurologic care in May of 2019?
A: Is this signed by the neurologist? Because I said that he refused to see neurology.

Q: But when you said that, you meant to see an actual neurologist, not neurologic care?
A: Right. MR. TREVISANI: Can we take this down and pull up BUR 00004172. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This is Exhibit 15. Sharing screen. You have control. (Exhibit 15 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. This one is a little harder to read, but this is Jerome Burgess. It's another neurology clinic flow sheet. And across here, there are various dates. These look like 2015, 2016, 2016, 2017 and over to 2019. So, again, you agree that on these dates, he was receiving neurologic care?
A: He was if you allow me to include pseudoseizures. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. Let's take this down.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) On Page 31 of your declaration, sort of in the middle of the page, Mr. Burgess also makes claims that he's consistently receiving self catheretization supplies, and then there's another sentence. And then the last sentence says, "I only found evidence of one informal grievance from him regarding this in April of 2016." Do you see that?
A: Uh-huh. I do. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. Can we bring up BUR 00004650. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. Exhibit 16. Sharing screen. MR. TREVISANI: Thank you. Give me one second. (Exhibit 16 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Could you read this, please?
A: There's a lot of this I can't read.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Well, let me just ask you a question. This is dated February 26, 2019, and right about here (indicating), he's complaining about not getting replacement catheters and that he has to reuse and reuse them; is that right?
A: It says that he can't use the catheters. So is he getting catheters that he can't or won't use or doesn't want to use? Or using the ones that he is familiar with? I can't make all this out.

Q: Well, all I know is --
A: In I any case --

Q: -- this is a -- I'm sorry. Go ahead.
A: In any case, I allowed in my opinion that there may have been times when he wasn't getting catheters appropriately, and that can happen in any institution. It happens with us from time to time getting our supplies perfectly right for each person. I guess you might -- is that any different in the restrictive housing versus GP? And my point is that it's the same supplier within the institution. It self-services the clinic storeroom, and the same nursing staff. So, you know, it would -- if they had run out of his preferred catheter, then that would be the case whether he was on GP or restrictive housing.

Q: This is a complaint about him got not getting catheters that is after April of 2016, isn't it? MS. SMITH: Overbroad; vague.
A: Again, I'm not -- okay. Sorry. MR. TREVISANI: And can you bring up the BUR 00011273. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This will be Exhibit 17.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) And I should ask, Dr. Paulson, do you remember seeing that grievance that we just saw?
A: I can't remember if it's the one that I saw. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: And you have control. (Exhibit 17 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. This is Exhibit 17. I'll make it bigger. Scroll down to the -- okay. Can you take a minute to read this one. And I'll ask you as you read this, so this is a complaint. One of his complaints is that he is having problems getting catheters while in CM at Suwannee; is that right?
A: He -- he is complaining having difficulty, many problems receiving them, that being his special catheters. I don't know if he was offered alternatives. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. We can take this down now.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. So these were -- these were, again -- do you remember seeing that complaint in your record review?
A: Again, I don't recall if that's the one I saw.

Q: Okay. So these -- but these were complaints about catheters. They came after April of 2016, correct? MS. SMITH: Overbroad.
A: I'll take your word on the date. I don't recall seeing that right now. I wasn't looking there.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Well -- okay. But so your statement here that you only found evidence of one informal grievance from him regarding this, being the catheters, in April of 2016 --
A: Uh-huh.

Q: -- that's not correct, right?
A: That is correct. That's -- that's what I found. I only found -- that is correct that that is what I found.

Q: I understand that's correct that's what found. But is that correct that there are records that postdate April of 2016?
A: You showed me two grievance forms, yeah. Is this formal or informal?

Q: I'm not sure.
A: Okay.

Q: Okay. So let's move to Mr. Kendrick on Page 30 -- let's see, Page 34 of your declaration. You have an opinion about Mr. Kendrick's weight loss. Do you know why Mr. Kendrick lost weight during that time?
A: I don't know.

Q: Okay. Is that something important that you think medical staff should look into?
A: Certainly if it got to be a substantial weight loss or -- or worse.

Q: Well, was Mr. Kendrick trying to lose weight during that period? MS. SMITH: Predicate.
A: I don't know.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Well, assuming he was not, isn't it a cause for concern when a patient losses that much weight without trying?
A: Generally we look at a substantial weight loss at a 10 percent. So people's weights vary, but people who are heavier vary more be. A 10 percent weight loss with him be 28 to 30 pounds.

Q: So this -- in your opinion, this is not something that needed further medical investigation?
A: Not unless it continued, unintended weight loss, unwanted weight loss for a period of time to where it became substantial. 13 pound variability in a 300-pound man, you know, that's -- that's not cause for alarm generally, but if it continued and he wasn't trying and it got to be more, then more. Now, if he was trying to lose weight, that be would a healthy weight loss, four pounds a week.

Q: You noted that Mr. Kendrick refused his insulin several times.
A: Are we on the next page?

Q: It's in that page and then again at the next page about insulin injections. MR. TREVISANI: And while you're looking at that, can we pull up KEN 00003767. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Stand by. This is Exhibit 18. (Exhibit 18 marked.) (BY MR. TREVISANI) Dr. Paulson --
A: Yes.

Q: -- do you remember seeing or -- seeing anything in the records indicating any reasons why Mr. Kendrick was refusing his insulin?
A: I don't remember that, no.

Q: Okay. This Exhibit 18, which is a grievance that he filed, can you take just a minute to read that.
A: Yes, I do remember reading this.

Q: Okay. So in this one, he's complaining that he's getting his insulin but that his food is not getting delivered until more than an hour later, which can be dangerous for from a medical perspective; is that right?
A: It's -- the danger for medical perspective would depend.

Q: Okay. Well, is it dangerous for Mr. Kendrick?
A: I don't know. I don't know what all types of insulin that he's getting. Certainly the NPH wouldn't be dangerous and regular insulin probably not either, and I don't know how closely his blood sugars are under control at this point in time. If he's under very close control, he might become somewhat symptomatic with a large amount of regular insulin. Although, most people an hour or so with regular insulin is be not a big deal, which is the reason we use regular insulin and the other longer lasting ones like NPH and Lantus, just because they don't bottom people out quickly because the meals at our institution can vary. There could be a fight kitchen and everybody is two hours late. You don't want your diabetics falling out. So it would depend.

Q: Okay. And then so did you read here that he says, "Grievant asserts that when he refuses his injections because of this highly dangerous practice, it is recorded in his medical records as being noncompliant"? So I guess my question is, did you take this into account when assessing his refusals of insulin injections?
A: Did I take this into account? I read this and that seems to be his reasoning for this period of time. But I don't know whether or not they've counseled him about his insulin and the safety of it regarding time is his general control, where this fits into how closely controlled he is.

Q: If he -- I guess my question is, if he indeed refused --
A: Uh-huh.

Q: -- because of this reason, you wouldn't consider that to be -- well, let me ask, you wouldn't consider that be to a true refusal of health care, correct?
A: If that was -- if that was a -- if that was a refusal for a patient I didn't know and had never had never counseled and there's no evidence in the -- in the chart that anyone had talked to be him about, I would bring him up and talk him to about it, or go down there and talk to him about it, if he's a CM patient and -- and try and reassure him that this is indeed not dangerous. If he hasn't bottomed out, he's not likely to bottom out. Certainly let us know if you feel badly, and find out, you know, what his reasoning is and what his fears are on try to work with those.

Q: Did that happen here?
A: I don't know. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. Can we take this one down. And can we bring up KEN 00003769? THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This is will be Exhibit 19. Sharing screen. You have control. (Exhibit 19 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. I am going to scroll down to Mr. Kendrick's grievance. If you could take a minute and read that. THE WITNESS: Can you roll it down a bit. It's blocked by the by the video boxes. That's good. Okay. Can you roll back up again? That's good.
A: Okay.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. So here he's complaining that the nurse brought him the wrong insulin; is that right?
A: Yes.

Q: And if the nurse -- if he has to sign a refusal form from this, you wouldn't consider that to be a true refusal health care, would you?
A: No. If there was -- if there was an honest -- or dishonest, rather. If there was a medication error, he would be completely within his rights of refusing and nothing more for it. The person goes back and gets the right insulin and injects him. But it's odd here he's complaining about the -- the syringes coming preloaded at the same time he's complaining about the nurse throwing it down in front of him. Well, which one is it?

Q: I think he might be talking about other instances. MR. TREVISANI: But we can take this one down, and this will be the last one for Kendrick. Can you bring up KEN 00005346. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This will be Exhibit 20. And you have control. (Exhibit 20 marked.) MR. TREVISANI: Thank you. (BY MR. TREVISANI) And I'm going to scroll down to here. Could you read Mr. Kendrick's grievance here. Let me know if I need to move it.
A: We're good. Okay.

Q: Okay. So in this one he refused insulin because it was the wrong time; is that right?
A: I read it that the timing to his dinner --

Q: Right, exactly.
A: Okay. No.

Q: So my question is, if you saw this refusal, that he refused, he signed a refusal of this insulin --
A: Uh-huh.

Q: -- this would be not be indicative -- this would not be indicative of a true medical -- refusal of medical care, correct?
A: It would depend.

Q: Okay. Well, he's not refusing his insulin. He just -- he doesn't want to take it at a time that he thinks it is dangerous for him; is that right?
A: Yes, that is what he says. But I wonder, since this is more, have they talked to him about it and the fact that the NPH insulin has a long activity and a long -- I'm trying to look for the pharmacology of it. In any case -- in any case, the NPH takes a number of hours to peak. It is practically irrelevant the timing that you're taking it, particularly if you're taking more than once a day, to your meals. So --

Q: But do you think --
A: If someone had explained that to him and showed him -- I'll even show people that the PDR information about -- about the medication, you know, look, this one doesn't peak for 12 hours, and it last for 24, and you're taking it twice a day so it's smooth all the through the day and night it's going to make you bottom out no matter what time you eat. Just make sure you eat and eat healthfully and take care of yourself and get your exercise. If despite doing that and knowing that he understood what I said, he complains about meal times, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't -- I would take that as a mealtime complaint, not a medication complaint.

Q: So did anybody in Florida Department of Corrections do what you suggested and try to figure out why Mr. Kendrick was refusing his insulin?
A: I don't know. You didn't -- you didn't let me see the response.

Q: Oh, okay. Well, do you want to see it?
A: All right. So it showed that he -- they reminded him that he would not get in trouble, and that he was refusing his blood sugar checks and refusing his metformin. They did contact the kitchen, that's good. What does it say -- oh, yep, you have an upcoming appointment to discuss with your clinician, so they were going to the right thing for him even if they had done it before. I don't know if his clinician had talked to him before about this, but that was their response this time. I'm not sure what their response to the previous one was. But even if this was his first time of refusing his insulin for the timing, mealtime purpose, this looks like the right thing to do, including having him see his clinician to discuss it. And then he can discuss it and say, hey, the timing doesn't matter as far as your insulin and your health with the type of insulins that you're taking. Do -- you know, work your best with all the things you can do, including taking your metformin, yeah. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. Can we take this down. And now might be a good time to take a five-minute Back at 5:36. (Break taken from 5:31 p.m. to 5:38 p.m.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) All right. So the homestretch. Let's talk about Mr. Espinosa.
A: Okay. Can I quickly jump in. I took the moment to refresh myself on N.P.H. insulin. It peaks at six to eight hours after the -- after the injection and lasts for 12 to 16 hours, so if you're taking it twice a day, it just doesn't matter when you eat and if you want it to match the peak, you would eat six hours after the injection. But the peaks and valleys are very mild and it's not like cascade mountain peaks that we have here, it's more like Florida mountain peaks. So -- so explaining to him once or twice, after that I would say that he's just -- he's just levering to try and get his meals differently or get snacks or something else. But this is something that could be easily explained and put his mind at ease if his mind is troubled.

Q: Okay. Do you know if that was explained to him?
A: I don't know.

Q: So moving on to Mr. Espinosa, Page 38 of your declaration.
A: Okay.

Q: Do you have an opinion on whether his inability to speak is caused by functional aphasia versus some other organic cause from his throat?
A: I rather think it's a functional aphasia based on the evidence from his endoscopy and his MRI, and laryngoscopy and multiple biopsies.

Q: You would -- you would agree that even if he has functional aphasia, he is unable to speak?
A: No, I wouldn't agree.

Q: Okay. How would you describe it?
A: I -- he -- he might be unable to speak if -- if his functional aphasia was from a serious and ongoing mental illness just like someone with schizophrenia can't control their hallucinations, but then that might be able to come under control with good psychiatric care. But there are a lot people where it's not a true conversion disorder, just a choice not to speak. And I gave an example in my -- from my little practice.

Q: Did the Department of Corrections medical staff attempt to determine whether -- well, strike that. Is the DOC mental health staff, are they treating him for functional aphasia? MS. SMITH: Scope. Predicate.
A: That, I don't know.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Do you think that the DOC mental health staff or the medical staff should be pursuing whether Mr. Espinosa needs mental health treatment because of functional aphasia? MS. SMITH: Scope.
A: I don't know whether or not they've assessed him for a major mental health disorder such as a conversion reaction or persistent conversion. But from -- from an allopathic medical standpoint, from my medical standpoint, I treat my patients how they are. He's not speaking, I'm treating him as though he's not speaking is enough.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) But my question is whether or not they have evaluated him. You agree that they should evaluate him, correct? MS. SMITH: Predicate. Scope.
A: If he -- if -- if they have been referred by the -- by his primary doctors, most certainly. I don't know if they have had another explanation for it or what the circumstances was there that would be more kibitzing than I have information to use for deciding.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Right. But you agree that somebody should try to figure that out, right?
A: Yeah. It could be his primary doctor didn't see any evidence of -- of major mental health and continued to treat him as a functional aphasia.

Q: Okay. And you agree that if he does have functional aphasia, that that's a serious mental health problem?
A: No. For some people it's a choice.

Q: Well, I thought you explained to me that for some people it's a choice, but true functional aphasia is a mental health disorder?
A: No. A conversion disorder which can cause functional aphasia is -- is a major health -- a major mental health disorder. But that's rather rare and, particularly, they have it last for a long period of time. And what I'm getting at is I'm not saying that he doesn't have any mental health disorder. But it's not necessarily contributing or causing his -- his functional aphasia and shouldn't interfere with his medical treatment one way or the other. He should be cared for properly, regardless of whether he is speaking or not speaking or know the reason for speaking or not speaking.

Q: Did you review any of Mr. Espinosa's mental health records?
A: I would have at least thumbed through them because they're intertwined with his medical record and other things.

Q: Okay. Let's talk about Brandon Welch.
A: What page are we on?

Q: I'm looking for it. It's Page 21 of your declaration?
A: Oh, here they are. Okay. Never mind. All right. Got you. MR. TREVISANI: And can we pull up, while we're waiting, PIR00069789. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. 69789? MR. TREVISANI: Yes, I think so. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: I never did receive that one. MR. TREVISANI: How about PIR00067 -- 69731. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: That's it. I do have that one. MR. TREVISANI: Thank you. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand -- please stand by. And this would be Paulson 21. Sharing screen. And you have got control. MR. TREVISANI: Thank you. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Uh-huh. MR. TREVISANI: So this is actually -- okay, now I know why I gave you the first one. This is a longer document. So I'm going to scroll to PIR00069731. Merinda, is there a way to go to a particular page of the PDF here (indicating)? THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Yes. Right there, type in the page number. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. Okay. This is the one I was looking for. (Exhibit 21 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) So this is, for the record -- well, no, it's the next one. My bad. Never mind. 6978. And this is a fracture dislocation sprain protocol. So Mr. Welch was involved in some kind of altercation. He says he got hit. It involved a lock and a sock and -- let's see. And the -- the date on this is July 13th, 2020; is that right? Do you see that here?
A: Oh, yes, I see that.

Q: Okay. And down here under findings there's a checkbox, and the patient has possible fracture and/or dislocation; do you see that?
A: Yes.

Q: Okay. And then over here he's reporting 7 out of 10 pain. And -- okay. So -- so the nurse notes a possible fracture and/or dislocation. And then according to your declaration, he wasn't seen until September 14th of 2020, so it's about two months later; is that right?
A: I have it he was X-rayed on September 14th.

Q: Okay. Do you know why it took two months to get him the X-ray?
A: No, I don't.

Q: All right. Is that an appropriate delay considering that the nurse noted a possible fracture and/or dislocation two months earlier?
A: It -- it would have been appropriate to -- to have -- he received a pain referral for dental to have it X-rayed, I think is what it said; am I right? And that would be appropriate to have that in a reasonable period of time.

Q: But two months is appropriate?
A: No. The -- the immediate referral for dental and -- but then to have that in an appropriate period of time in a few days. It depend -- it depends somewhat on the -- on the circumstance of the injury and how it looked, if there was -- if the teeth were malaligned, if there was break in the skin, if there was a -- a visible external malalignment, somewhat swelling, that general tenderness without -- without -- without focus, teeth that are aligned properly, no internal or external bleeding, and no palpable step off, that's less of a problem. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. We can take this down.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Other than the opinions that we've already discussed today, are there any other opinions that you intend to offer regarding Plaintiff's motion for class certification or the evidence in support of that motion?
A: Nothing that comes to mind.

Q: Do you plan to do any other work on this case?
A: Only if -- if Nicole asks me to.

Q: But right now you have no further plans to do any further work?
A: No, I don't have anything in front of me on this case.

Q: Okay. How many hours have you spent on this case so far, do you know?
A: Oh, no idea. Quite a few.

Q: Do you know how much you've billed the Department of Corrections so far?
A: No. But there are quite a few hours.

Q: Is there anything that you wanted to see, but you were not able to see?
A: No.

Q: Any information that you wanted, but didn't get?
A: No. MR. TREVISANI: Can you bring up -- hopefully I have it -- EHA01266865. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. EHA01266865, correct? MR. TREVISANI: Yes. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Okay. Exhibit 22. Share screen. You have control. (Exhibit 22 marked.)

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Scrolling down, this is an e-mail from Cayla Moseley dated May 10th, 2021 to you, Reed Paulson. And it says, "Good morning, Dr. Paulson, below is a ShareFile link containing programs the department partook in, data was created to track that -- was created to track those programs, and Juan Espinosa's deposition." What are the programs the department partook in and the data that was created to track these programs? What is that referring to?
A: I don't recall. MR. TREVISANI: Okay. You can take this down.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Do you recall seeing any documents related to an alternative segregation pilot?
A: Documents. Yeah, there was something. But I really don't remember any details of it. It was something that was being proposed or we were going to try or -- I don't know.

Q: Did you have any discussions with FDC staff about an alternative segregation pilot?
A: No.

Q: Okay. What about any documents related to the analysis of the segregation process, do you remember those documents?
A: I don't remember. MR. TREVISANI: I think that's all I have, Doctor. Thank you for your time. THE WITNESS: No, thank you. MS. SMITH: Thank you. We will read. (Off-the-record discussion.) THE COURT REPORTER: So this is due in three days, so Monday I was told. Is that true for you, Mr. Trevisani? MR. TREVISANI: I think -- I think unfortunately that is true. THE COURT REPORTER: Oh, no, no, I just -- and then, Ms. Smith, did you want to receive it then at the same time? MS. SMITH: We just need a regular delivery. We don't need anything expedited. (End of proceedings at 5:56 p.m.)

Q: Good morning, Dr. Paulson.
A: Good morning.

Q: Could you tell us where you are right now?

A: No.

Q: Okay. I'm going to go over a couple of basics for the deposition. One is, especially with the Zoom, you have to make sure to respond orally so that the court reporter can take it down. Make sure to wait until I finish the question before you answer so we don't talk over each other. And if you don't understand any of the questions, just let me know. I will try to rephrase it. But if you don't say anything, I'm going to assume that you understood the question. Is that okay?
A: Yes.

Q: Okay. Did you bring -- do you have any documents in -- with you there in the room that you intend to refer to during the deposition?

Q: Great. Do you have a copy of your declaration?
A: Yes. That, I have right here.

Q: Okay. Do you have any other documents that you relied on for your opinion available to you on the computer?
A: Not easily so.

Q: Okay. So other than your declaration, do you have any other documents there with you?
A: I have -- this was not in my declaration, though. I have a report from the recordations concerning the use of restrictive housing from the Department of Justice, 2016.

Q: Okay. Anything else?
A: That's it.

Q: Okay. MR. TREVISANI: Merinda, could we bring up Exhibit DHA01210933, which should be Dr. Paulson's CV. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This will be Exhibit 1, Paulson 1. MR. TREVISANI: Yes. Thank you. (Exhibit 1 marked.) THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: It's there on the screen. Would you like control? MR. TREVISANI: Yes, please. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: You have control. (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Dr. Paulson, I'm going to scroll through here. I'm going to make it a little bit bigger here for you.

A: Okay.

Q: -- I can give it to you, if you need to. But let me just scroll through it here.
A: All right.

Q: And, unfortunately, all the page numbers seem to be 2, but the last Bates number is DHA01210945. Is this your current CV, Dr. Paulson?
A: What I could see looks like it, yes.

Q: Okay. I want to ask you a couple of questions about your background. You received a master's in public health in 1990; is that right?
A: Yes.

Q: Did any of that training for your master's in public health involve any correctional medicine training?
A: Not directly so.

Q: Okay. How about indirectly?
A: I -- the -- my focus for that was in program planning.

Q: Okay. What's program planning?
A: It's, essentially, the -- like it sounds. It's putting together and writing programs for medical circumstances.

Q: Okay. And then here, it says you received a master's training in research 1978-1980.
A: Yes.

Q: What is that degree?
A: That was in neurophysiology.

Q: And then, going down to your residency, did your residency have any particular specialty?
A: Family medicine.

Q: And did that involve any training or experience with correctional medicine?
A: To some extent. A lot of it was emergency room. Also, the County of Los Angeles had both a sheriff's office and -- it was a hospital of choice for hospitalizations regarding inmates for that portion of Los Angeles.

Q: But you treated those people in a hospital, right?
A: In hospital, yes.

Q: You didn't treat them in the jail?
A: No.

Q: Okay. And then scrolling down on your CV, to -- in 2019, it says, "Certified Correctional Health Care Provider - Physician," from the "National Commission on Correctional Health Care." Can you tell me about that certification?
A: That certification involves two -- two prerequisite certifications and is about essentially being familiar with and reasons for the various standards that the NCCHC holds for jails and prisons.
05_chunk_0001.title: 05 (chunk 2/61)

05_chunk_0002.text:
on?
A: That certification involves two -- two prerequisite certifications and is about essentially being familiar with and reasons for the various standards that the NCCHC holds for jails and prisons.

Q: So what do you have to do to become eligible for the certification?
A: Study and -- and take an exam.

Q: Is there any experience requirement?
A: Let me think. I don't recall.

Q: Have you published any papers in any peer-reviewed journals?
A: No.

Q: Have you conducted any research in correctional medicine?
A: Not other than in -- in quality assurance in my position as chief medical officer of the Oregon State Penitentiary.

Q: Okay. And so you haven't also conducted any research in health care provided in solitary confinement?
A: Not published, no.

Q: Okay. And same question. You haven't conducted any research on health care provided to people in restrictive housing?
A: Not published, no.

Q: And is there unpublished research?
A: Well, like I said, doing the quality assurance and monitoring in our own system.

Q: So it looks like you started with the Oregon Department of Corrections in 2009. Is that right?
A: That sounds right.

Q: All right. I'm looking for the -- ah, give me a second. There we go. Okay. So why did you take that job?
A: Number of reasons. I'd been working emergency most of my career. And I was in my mid 50s, and the nights were killing me. That was probably the biggest one. I had a young family, and I was missing recitals and things, because it's a 24/7 matter. So I was looking for, primarily, something that didn't have night and weekend work. I knew two physicians who had worked for the department. One ran -- that I worked with as a colleague in the same clinic for a number of years, and another that I graduated from medical school with. Both had worked, and one of them was continuing to work, with the Oregon Department of Corrections.

Q: So your current job is chief medical officer for the Oregon State Penitentiary; is that right?
A: Yes, but I'm in transition.

Q: And what's the transition?
A: I'm transitioning to retiring. So I'm not seeing patients directly in clinic at this point. I'm consulting on lots of cases. And they haven't replaced me as chief medical officer yet. But when they do, I'll stop those duties.

Q: Okay. So I want to talk to you --
A: (Inaudible) sometime next year.

Q: Understood. So I want to talk about your job throughout your time at the Oregon State Penitentiary. Have you had the same job from 2009 to the present?
A: I've -- I've -- the position of the correctional medi- -- pardon me -- correctional physician specialist in the department gives us ability to move from -- from site to site. So my job has been the same, but I have had different sites.

Q: So in this whole time, were you the chief medical officer for the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: No.

Q: Okay. So what years were you the chief medical officer for the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: That, I always have to think a bit about. It's been, I think, the last six, almost seven, years.

Q: So when you came to the Oregon Department of Corrections in 2009, what was your job?
A: My job was to be a physician on -- on staff there.

Q: Okay. So -- and then, did you have any other jobs before you transitioned to becoming the chief medical officer of the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: Well, within my duties there, I was a physician in charge of direct care to the segregated housing units and mental health infirmary, Death Row, behavioral health unit. I continued that for a while when I was the chief medical officer. Also, I had the same, similar duties at Coffee Creek, what would be on your -- you covered multiple places, but -- and I can't remember. It's probably -- I was chief medical officer for a year or so when we finally got another staff member and I was able to -- to hand over the segregation and mental health unit's medical care.

Q: So what years were you responsible for the medical care in the segregation units and the mental health care?
A: That, again, I have to think. Because for two years, I was working -- I was covering both Coffee Creek, which is the intake center and women's prisons, and OSP. And somewhere in that two-year period, I was transitioning from one to the other and was able to take up the duties. So that would have been around 2012 or '13, I think. No. '13, '14. Again, it's just a guess.
05_chunk_0002.title: 05 (chunk 3/61)

05_chunk_0003.text:
here in that two-year period, I was transitioning from one to the other and was able to take up the duties. So that would have been around 2012 or '13, I think. No. '13, '14. Again, it's just a guess.

Q: Okay. And then, I think you said that you became chief medical officer of the Oregon State Penitentiary roughly six or seven years ago?
A: Yes.

Q: So does 2015 sound about right?
A: 2014, 2015, something like that. It's when Dr. Degner retired. Again, since my position doesn't change, I don't have -- you don't apply for these -- these changes. Our -- our credentialing, essentially, is continuous through them. It's just what I'm doing on a particular day. And like I said, it -- there isn't a new job description, essentially, that comes from our -- my -- my position has been the same position with the department the whole time.

Q: And that position is correctional physician specialist?
A: Yeah, correctional physician specialist.

Q: So during the time that you were the chief medical officer, what were your duties and responsibilities?
A: It's -- it's largely about working to get the best medical care possible. I work with the physicians and nurse practitioners, PAs when we have them, as a -- as a resource. Essentially, it's like being a lead worker. I've got the most experience, both in practice and in the department. And on top of that, the -- there's a certain amount of QA that's done and a certain amount of -- of review of records that -- where there's a problem, and a certain amount of oversight for the mental health section, particularly in the area of involuntary medication.

Q: QA is quality assurance?
A: Yes.

Q: Is it fair to say that you're responsible for all the medical care provided at the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: No.

Q: Is there a person who is responsible for that?
A: We have licensed medical professionals being responsible for themselves.

Q: So does the chief medical officer -- are you the highest-ranking medical person at Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: It's not a ranking. Like I said, I'm essentially lead worker, there to give people help, to -- to make things better. I don't hire or fire anyone. I don't write anyone's performance review. The department has a medical director, but that's not me. And it's a really good thing, because that way, I'm not a threat to anybody. I'm just helping them do better medicine for our patients.

Q: Does anybody report to you?
A: Not report in the sense that -- that their job is -- that I'm responsible for their job. No. Like I said, I don't write anyone's performance reviews.

Q: Who do you report to?
A: To -- to the medical director.

Q: And is the medical director somebody who's at the Oregon State Penitentiary, or are they medical director for the entire Oregon Department of Corrections?
A: The director is over all the facilities.

Q: The entire Department of Corrections?
A: Yes.

Q: Do you have any responsibility for setting medical policy at Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: The policies and procedures, I've had input in that over the years. I've written several. And so in that regard, it's kind of a -- we're a small department, so everyone has a say. And like I said, I've -- I've been a writer on several of them in the past. I haven't done any lately.

Q: Okay. What percentage of your job now is treating patients?
A: I don't see patients directly at all right now.

Q: Okay. When did you stop seeing patients?
A: September.

Q: And so before September, what percentage of your job was treating patients?
A: Oh. Well, 100 percent, essentially, since I've never had carved-out, formal time for the chief medical officer work.

Q: Okay. So do you have any administrative responsibilities as the chief medical officer?
A: A certain amount of quality assurance and overseeing cases where there's -- there's a question of care, something like that. I'm generally the first person to look at that and -- within our -- our facility.

Q: What does the quality assurance look like?
A: The -- a quality assurance committee for health services in OSP. I'm the physician sitting on that -- that small committee. We do reviews of areas, some of them rotating and some of them permanent, essentially charted use of cases. The rotating ones are generally random. The permanent ones, like I -- I review -- review every death, every hospitalization where I can't get the record before the patient is transferred. And a certain amount of the emergency transfers, medical emergency transfers.
05_chunk_0003.title: 05 (chunk 4/61)

05_chunk_0004.text:
I -- I review -- review every death, every hospitalization where I can't get the record before the patient is transferred. And a certain amount of the emergency transfers, medical emergency transfers.

Q: Are there any regular audits of the medical care provided at Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: Like I said, there -- there's rotating quality assurance audits. And the department and OSP are part of the NCCHC, and they audit periodically.

Q: Okay. And the internal audits, are they conducted by Oregon Department of Corrections staff?
A: Yes. Well, there's the quality assurance audits we're talking about, yeah.

Q: Have you worked in any other correctional setting, other than the Oregon State Penitentiary?
A: Just what's listed in my CV and my introduction declaration.

Q: Do you have any expertise in prison administration outside of the medical context?
A: No.

Q: What about, do you have any expertise in running a solitary confinement unit?
A: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the last part.

Q: Do you have any expertise in running a solitary confinement unit? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: Only in the medi- -- provision of medical care.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Going down to the page on your CV -- or, I guess, up, rather, there is a list here of various cases. And it looks like -- it looks like there are 10 cases listed there. Are those cases where you've served as an expert witnesses?
A: Yes.

Q: Are there any other than the ones that are listed here?
A: Is the last one -- is Harvard in there?

Q: Do you mean this case --
A: Yes.

Q: -- that we're on right now? Well, other than this case that we're on taking this deposition.
A: That needs to be added. And I'm just taking on another case right now that I'll work on after the first of the year.

Q: Okay. So other than that one and the Harvard case, there's none other than these that are listed here?
A: Correct.

Q: And then, it looks like, under correctional medical expert file depository experience here, there's this Hamblin case. And then it looks like the case is listed again in the second section here, Hamblin. Is that the same case?
A: Yes.

Q: And in any of these cases, did you give a deposition?
A: Well, in the Hamblin case.

Q: (Inaudible) other?
A: (No response.)

Q: Are there any other cases where you gave a deposition?
A: Yes. They're listed in my declaration.

Q: Okay. Can you tell me which ones?
A: Hamblin. Rojas versus Correct Care Solutions. The Estate of John Kleutsch versus State of Washington. Alejandro Gallegos versus K. Seeley. And, of course, this one right now.

Q: Okay. And did you testify at trial in any of those cases?
A: No.

Q: In the ones where you did not provide -- or you did not give a deposition, did you prepare an expert report?
A: Can you scroll down so I can see more?

Q: Sure.
A: It's easier to give you the exceptions. I have not given a report for Ramey or Carol Cole. The Carol Cole was a case that I dropped out of after reviewing. So that one, I didn't have any involvement past first review.

Q: Okay. Were -- were any of these -- in any of these cases, where you've been an expert, where you were retained by the plaintiff?
A: Yes. This list, Kleutsch, Thomsen, Widmayer. Can you roll on down. Rojas, Ramey, Perry, Hamblin and Ale- -- Gallegos.

Q: Okay. So was that all of them that -- where you were retained by the plaintiff?
A: All on this list, yes. I don't think this list is complete. This lists -- CV is -- could use some updating at this point.

Q: Oh. Well, that's why I asked you, are there any others that are listed here? I thought you told me there were not.
A: There's none that are -- there's none -- I'm sorry. I might have misunderstood you. These -- this list is somewhat old and doesn't include everything.

Q: Okay. So what are the other cases where you've been retained by an expert?
A: I would have to -- I would have to go to memory at this point, and I don't think I could give it accurately without looking through my records.

Q: Well, approximately how many are there, other than the ones --
A: It might be another two or three.
05_chunk_0004.title: 05 (chunk 5/61)

05_chunk_0005.text:
at this point, and I don't think I could give it accurately without looking through my records.

Q: Well, approximately how many are there, other than the ones --
A: It might be another two or three.

Q: Okay. So what percentage of the time, in all of the cases where you've been retained as an expert, were you retained by the plaintiff versus the defendant?
A: Oh, perhaps 75 or 80 percent.

Q: That was -- the 75, 80 percent was the plaintiff?
A: Were the plaintiffs, yes.

Q: Okay. These all -- these all -- the ones that are listed here -- well, I guess, let me ask it a different way. The cases where you've been retained as an expert, were they all involving one individual plaintiff seeking damages?
A: Yes.

A: Can you -- can you define what you mean there by "like"?

A: Well, a lot of cases involve looking at the system, but -- because, a lot of times, then, problems might arise from more than just a medical provider, such as transport or other administrative issues that are part of an individual case. But these -- these have all been individual cases with an -- where an individual inmate is part of the -- the question.

Q: That's what I'm asking. Are there any other cases where you're asking to evaluate a system, not for the care provided to one individual, but for the system as a whole?
A: No.

Q: So this Harvard case, this is the first time that you've done that? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: And let me -- let me extend that a little bit. I obviously help my department in that -- in cases of -- involving our department. And some of those have -- have been regarding the system. But, again, those -- this isn't the same thing as we've been talking about, being retained as an expert.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Any of the cases where you've been retained as an expert in the past, did the -- did those cases involve medical care that was being provided in solitary confinement or restrictive housing?
A: Yes.

Q: Which ones?
A: Well, let me look at this list. Thomsen, Widmayer. Can you roll -- scroll down? Ramey, Perry. That's it.

Q: Have you ever been excluded as an expert by a court?
A: No.

Q: Has the court -- has a court ever limited your testimony or your opinions?
A: No.

Q: Have you ever served as an expert for the Florida Department of Corrections before?
A: No.

Q: Have you ever been retained by the Rumberger Kirk law firm before?
A: No. MR. TREVISANI: If you could take down this exhibit.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) How did you first become involved with this case?
A: I believe I got an e-mail from one of the lawyers at Rumberger Kirk.

Q: Okay. And what were you asked to do for the case?
A: I was asked to review the medical care, and particularly regarding the complaint involved.

Q: Uh-huh. And what was your -- what was your assignment, so to speak?
A: Essentially, the area of allopathic medicine.

Q: Well, I mean, I guess I'm asking, what were you asked to do? What were you asked to give an opinion?
A: About the areas in the complaint, and -- and to review the medical care of the -- of the plaintiffs.

Q: Do you have some kind of retainer letter or engagement letter?
A: No. I think there are medical privacy letters, but I don't think there was a formal retainer letter.

Q: When were you retained?
A: Late winter. Mid-winter. Yeah. January, February, I believe.

Q: Of what year?
A: 2020 -- 2021.

Q: What did you do to prepare for today's deposition?
A: In -- in -- I've read through various pieces of information regarding the case, part -- things in the list. In particular, some of the plaintiffs' depositions and the particulars of my declaration, the Third Amended Complaint, and that's about it.

Q: Did you speak to anybody to prepare for the deposition?
A: No. MR. TREVISANI: Can we bring up an exhibit. It's called Dr. Reed Paulson Declaration. THE REMOTE TECHNICIAN: Please stand by. This would be Paulson Exhibit 2. MR. TREVISANI: Yes. Thank you. Q: Do you think it would be more or less than general population? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: It -- it -- the -- I wouldn't know because there are different size populations with different needs.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) When the patients in restrictive housing in Florida are seen in medical, are they fully restrained? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: That's a security question.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) So do you know the answer?
A: I imagine the answer is they're restrained appropriate for their circumstances.

Q: Does having a patient be fully restrained make it harder to provide medical care to them?
A: Can you define "fully restrained" for me?

Q: Well, let's say handcuffed and leg chains.
A: And what was your question again? I'm sorry.

Q: Is it harder to provide medical care to that person when they're fully restrained?
A: Not especially.

Q: It's just the same as if they were not, they were not restrained?
A: Pretty much. If there's any problem and it involves one of the limbs, then we have to work with that, you know, asking if -- you do what you can with the restraints in place, which is quite a lot generally, and then working with security to see if that limb can be uncuffed and examined, something like that. It's really no big deal. Like I say, I spent most of my career in the emergency room and when the sheriffs bring someone in, they're in cuffs, sometimes cuffs and shackles, sometimes with a Taser wire still on them.

Q: When inmates in restrictive housing in Florida are seen in medical, is an officer present in the exam room?
A: I don't -- I don't know in particular, and I'm sure it would somewhat depend on the circumstance but I wouldn't be surprised at all.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Is that kind of knowledge, is that important to forming your opinion in this case?
A: No, that's a security issue.

Q: Okay. And do you think it's, in your experience, is a -- does having a security officer in the room make the medical examination more difficult?
A: Not in my experience.
05_chunk_0013.title: 05 (chunk 14/61)

05_chunk_0014.text:
, that's a security issue.

Q: Okay. And do you think it's, in your experience, is a -- does having a security officer in the room make the medical examination more difficult?
A: Not in my experience.

Q: Does it make the patient less likely to be candid?
A: I have no way of knowing whether or not someone is telling me the truth.

Q: Well, if somebody is less candid, that is going to affect the medical care that you provide them; is that right?
A: I haven't found it to be a problem.

Q: Well, I'm not asking if you found candor to be a problem. I'm saying, if somebody is -- doesn't want to be fully candid, that can affect the medical care that you provide to them, right?
A: Yes, it can. And it happens all the time no matter where we are.

Q: Because they might -- they might not give you the full story, right? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: Yes.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) And you need the full story to provide them with appropriate medical care? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: Sometimes you do. Sometimes I don't need a story at all.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) You need to interview the person, right?
A: I always do but -- but there are times when the interview really doesn't add much to the circumstance, such as looking at a sore throat.

Q: Okay. Could you take a look at Page 7 of your declaration?
A: Uh-huh. Got it.

Q: And the paragraph right in the middle, it says, "The preconfinement and post-use-of-force evaluations were consistently done to American Correctional Association, ACA, standards and reasonable and appropriate medical standards." Do you see that?
A: Yes.

Q: How did you reach that conclusion?
A: From looking at quite a number of post-use-of-force and preconfinement documentations.

Q: Okay. So would this -- were these the documentations that were within the individual sets of medical records that you reviewed?
A: Yes. I can't think of any that weren't.

Q: So what -- what you're relying on for that conclusion is the records, right?
A: Correct.

Q: You didn't actually observe whether these preconfinement and post-use-of-force evaluations were actually happening?
A: No. But I did have the record often beyond the -- beyond the preconfinement or post-use-of-force interview -- I'm sorry, evaluation. And that is useful information in that regard a lot of times.

Q: Okay. Backing up a little bit, just in general, how does someone in restrictive housing in Florida access health care? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: I think I discussed that in my declaration. They can make a sick call request in paper. They can mention it to the nurse that comes by each day. If they have an emergency, they can ask any staff.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) (Inaudible.) THE REPORTER: I'm sorry. I didn't hear that. MR. TREVISANI: Sorry. I think I was rattling paper. (BY MR. TREVISANI) How does an inmate in restrictive housing in Florida get a sick call form? THE COURT REPORTER: How do inmates in restrictive housing get? (BY MR. TREVISANI) Restrictive housing in Florida get a sick call form.
A: My understanding is they can request one from any of the staff, but often get it from the nurse that comes each day, but they can request it from the officers and other staff also.

Q: Okay. But they have to wait for someone to come around to request a sick call form, right?
A: It might be 29 minutes.

Q: And what are you referencing with the 29 minutes?
A: That the -- well, the officers are checking roughly every 30 minutes, so they've got another 29 to wait if they missed them a minute ago.

Q: And then what happens after that? They get the sick call form, they fill it out and then what?
A: They can turn it in either to the nurses that come the next day or to any of the officers.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. And then what's the next step?
A: They put it in with sick call forms, which are collected and gone through, and I assume sick call lists come from that.

Q: Okay. And then what's the next step in terms of how they get to medical or how are they seen? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: My understanding it's a process very similar to ours. They are reviewed by a nurse and appropriate steps taken for that, depending on what the request is and the circumstance.
