Objection; overbroad.
A: My understanding it's a process very similar to ours. They are reviewed by a nurse and appropriate steps taken for that, depending on what the request is and the circumstance.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. So what would the -- I am just trying to figure out, like, how does the inmate actually get seen? What's the next step? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad; asked and answered.
A: I'm sorry. I didn't get the whole question. You broke up.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) What's the next step after the sick call form is collected? MS. SMITH: Same objection.
A: As I said, the nurse goes through them each day and makes determinations of what's an appropriate next step.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. And what if the appropriate next step is that the inmate needs to have a medical examination, what happens?
A: It would depend on the medical examination that was felt to be needed individually.

Q: So would -- how would the -- that determination be made?
A: It would be -- it would be made by the registered nurse and his or her professional training.

Q: Okay. And what if the inmate needed to be seen in the medical facility, how would that work?
A: They would -- do you mean on a scheduled basis?

Q: Yes.
A: They would schedule an appointment.

Q: Okay. And then does how the inmate get from their cell to the appointment room?
A: They would be escorted by the officers.

Q: Okay. Now, similar questions for general population inmates. How do general population inmates in Florida access to health care?
A: As I understand it, they need to get -- first to get a sick call form. So they need to leave their cell and go to wherever those are, get one, fill it out someplace and then come to wherever the drop box is for dropping those off.

Q: The general population inmates in Florida, are they in individual cells?
A: You mean one per cell?

Q: Correct.
A: I'm sorry?

Q: Are general population inmates Florida housed in cells or are they in open-bay dorms?
A: I believe it's both.

Q: Okay. So for the general population inmates in open-bay dorms, are those sick call forms in the dorm for them to get?
A: That, I don't know for two reasons. I didn't go to all the dorms in all the places, and I only visited about one-tenth of the facilities.

Q: Well, you're offering an opinion comparing the access to medical care in restrictive housing versus general population, correct?
A: Correct.

Q: So you need to know how the medical care is accessed in general population, right?
A: Correct.

Q: So without that knowledge, you can't make that comparison, correct?
A: I did just explain how the sick call process is -- is -- is to go on in the Florida facilities. The inmate goes to where the form is, takes a form, goes back to where they can write, writes their sick call request, goes back to a drop box or wherever the forms are turned in to for their particular circumstance. And it goes on from there. That would be the same, dorm or not dorm, whether it's on the dorm or off the dorm. That's the process, as I understand it.

Q: And how is the process different from the process in restrictive housing?
A: The restrictive housing inmate doesn't have to go anywhere.

Q: They have to wait for somebody to come by to get the form, correct?
A: Correct.

Q: Could you -- if you could look at Page 8 of your declaration.
A: Yes.

Q: The second paragraph starts, quote, In contrast, general population, GP, inmates cannot simply walk over to the medical offices and meet with the nurse any time they want, unquote. I just want to be sure I understand what you're saying there because you agree that inmates in restrictive housing can't do that either, right?
A: No, they can't walk over to medical.

Q: Okay. So if -- if an inmate -- well, let me back up. If there are sick call forms available in a general population dorm at the officer station and the general population inmates can walk over and ask for one, it's easier for them to get those forms than somebody in restrictive housing who has to wait for somebody to come around. MS. SMITH: Objection; vague. (BY MR. TREVISANI) Do you agree?
A: That's your opinion of what easier is. The other -- other side of easier would be, I don't have to do anything other than stand up and take two steps to the door to get a form, and then fill out and go another two steps to the door to hand it in. That sounds easier to me.
05_chunk_0015.title: 05 (chunk 16/61)

would be, I don't have to do anything other than stand up and take two steps to the door to get a form, and then fill out and go another two steps to the door to hand it in. That sounds easier to me.

I'm asking about your opinion, which you have given an opinion that inmates in restrictive housing have better and more access to medical care. Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Your opinion is that it's easier to wait for somebody to come around to get a sick call form versus walking and getting one yourself?
A: My opinion is that they -- the restrictive housing inmate has an easier process as far as the ease of doing it. The waiting is trivial. Sometimes the walk is long and you -- depending on where things are. But I don't think that the difference in access is -- to the form is all that substantial.

Q: Going back to page 8 of your declaration, and I think you just mentioned it, when referencing general population inmates, you say that they can pick up their request form and then, quote, retreat to where the form can be filled out, unquote. What does that mean?
A: That means I'm -- in situations I'm aware of, oftentimes there isn't a pen and a desk at the site where the forms are that the inmate can fill out the form right there. Oftentimes they take their forms back to their cells where they have a desk and a pen and fill it out there.

Q: Do you know if that's true in Florida?
A: No.

Q: So if there are, in fact, pens and a desk where sick call forms are, then they wouldn't have to retreat to an area to fill it out; is that right?
A: No. They would just have to fill it out there at the desk, perhaps wait for their fellows to fill theirs out first. I'm sure there are a lot of different sets of circumstances. The facilities try to work things out for everything to work smoothly.

Q: And then where do inmates in general population drop the sick call form?
A: To wherever the drop station is.

Q: Do you know where they are?
A: No, I don't. MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) And then we covered this, but just to be clear, inmates in restrictive housing, to turn in the form, they have to wait for somebody to come around to turn it in, correct?
A: They -- they have to wait a trivial amount of time, yes.

Q: For inmates in general population in Florida, how long does it typically take from submitting a sick call form to being seen in medical? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: I don't know. And it would be -- it would depend on the circumstance.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Well, for inmates in restrictive housing in Florida, how long does it typically take from submission of a sick call form to being seen by medical? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: Same answer.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) In restrictive housing in Florida, do some medical appointments happen at cell front? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: As far as I'm aware, the only opportunity for that would be either a medical emergency where medical staff would respond to wherever the inmate was, including the workstation, or wherever, or restrictive housing where the nurse there -- the nurse is there once a day.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) So are you familiar with any instance where a nurse conducts any kind of medical evaluation in Florida in restrictive housing through the cell door? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: It's something that certainly could be done for certain circumstances and certain conditions.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) But in your opinion, it should not be the routine practice? MS. SMITH: Objection; vague.
A: It would depend on the medical issue and the circumstance.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Well, but -- so just to answer my question, like doing the cell-front medical evaluation should not be routine practice unless there's a reason to do it; is that fair? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: The care of the inmate should be appropriate regardless of where it's done. If someone wants to know what is this little thing right here (indicating). Well, you can't see my face that well. And the nurse can take a quick glance and say, oh, that's a skin tag, don't worry about it. That could be done through a cell door.
05_chunk_0016.title: 05 (chunk 17/61)

05_chunk_0017.text:
hing right here (indicating). Well, you can't see my face that well. And the nurse can take a quick glance and say, oh, that's a skin tag, don't worry about it. That could be done through a cell door.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) In general, in your opinion, do you think a medical examination through the cell door is better or worse than a medical examination face to face? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad and vague.
A: It would depend on the -- on the circumstance. I just gave you an example of something that would be perfectly adequate through the cell door. Now, realistically speaking, I would say that most things can't be done through the cell door, but you were asking me absolutes.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Why is that, that most things can't be done through the cell door?
A: Because most circumstances, in my experience, require more access than can be had through the cell door.

Q: And just to confirm, did you try to speak to any inmates through the cell door?
A: No, I did not.

Q: So you're not aware of how difficult or easy it is to hear through the door?
A: Well, I would have to -- have to qualify that a little bit. I said hi a few times just to be friendly, but nothing more substantial than that. I was able to see what the -- what the physical circumstances were in the various facilities and dorms and restrictive housing units.

Q: Did you assess how easy or hard it is to hear through the cell door?
A: Not formally, but I was around as officers talked to inmates through the cell doors as we were going through. It's not a difficult thing to figure out.

Q: Did you see -- well, back up. I think you testified that in many restrictive housing units, there is a medical group in the unit; is that right?
A: Correct.

Q: Did you see the inside of those units?
A: Are you talking about the unit in --

Q: I'm sorry. Let me rephrase that. Did you see the inside of those medical units?
A: Yes, many of them.

Q: And what's in those rooms typically?
A: Typically an exam table, lighting, a desk. Sometimes an ophthalmoscope on the wall, sometimes not. Sometimes blood pressure cuff, sometimes not. When those aren't, I assume that the nurse is bringing them. When they're doing their evaluations, that would be -- it would be a norm, but sometimes it's hanging on the wall. Portable lighting, things like that.

Q: In your opinion, are those rooms adequate for conducting medical examinations?
A: Yes. Many medical examinations, that would be adequate a lot of the time.

Q: Did you see the medical examination rooms in the medical clinics where -- or were they not in the medical wing?
A: Well, I saw quite a few of them.

Q: What's inside those medical examination rooms?
A: Many similar things, things that are appropriate to the average medical office.

Q: Is there more equipment in there or less equipment than the rooms, the medical rooms, in the restrictive housing units?
A: I can't say. My guess would be less.

Q: Less in which ones? I'm sorry.
A: Less in the restrictive housing units, the ones that I saw of each. I didn't make a -- a survey of that in particular that I could attest that that's an absolute.

Q: Okay. Can you turn to Page 9 of your declaration?
A: Yes.

Q: I want to -- okay. About the third or fourth sentence, there's a sentence that says, "A nurse will respond to their location immediately any time they think they have a medical emergency with no cost, no penalty if they overuse the privilege." Do you see that sentence?
A: Yes.

Q: I want to ask about the "no cost" language. Florida inmates have to pay copayments for medical, right?
A: I understand for certain things, they do.

Q: Okay. So would -- do you know how much the copayment is?
A: No, I don't. But if you read my sentence, it says, "with no cost and no penalty if they overuse the privilege."

Q: So I want to be -- that's why I'm asking you. I want to clarify what you said. I mean, do they have a cost to see medical, correct?
A: I was referring to overusing the privilege.

Q: Well, that's what I'm asking about. If an inmate submits a sick call request --
A: There's no extra cost for -- no extra cost for an overuse.
05_chunk_0017.title: 05 (chunk 18/61)

05_chunk_0018.text:
orrect?
A: I was referring to overusing the privilege.

Q: Well, that's what I'm asking about. If an inmate submits a sick call request --
A: There's no extra cost for -- no extra cost for an overuse.

Q: Beyond the copayment, correct?
A: I would assume so. I don't know they -- if it has the copay for a declared emergency or not.

Q: Okay. So we touched on this a little bit. We talked a little bit about the preconfinement physical. And do you agree that it's important for somebody to do, to get the preconfinement physical before being put in restrictive housing?
A: Are you referring to a preconfinement medical evaluation?

Q: Yes.
A: Okay. Because that's not necessarily a physical.

Q: Right. Thank you for correcting me. So do you think it's important for something -- somebody to get the preconfinement medical evaluation before going into restrictive housing in Florida?
A: It's often important.

Q: Why is it important?
A: So that the staff can look for things where -- that -- where restrictive housing might need to be altered, such as an ADA situation, or that they have conditions that need more intense nursing, such as someone who has medications three times a day, or insulin, things like that.

Q: So why is it particularly important to do it before going into restrictive housing versus, say, just going to another general population dorm? THE WITNESS: Are you there? MR. TREVISANI: I'm here. THE WITNESS: Okay. You fell off my video, but I see it in the other spot. I'm sorry. Can you repeat the question? (BY MR. TREVISANI) Why is it particularly important to do it before going into restrictive housing versus, say, going to another dorm in general population?
A: Because they -- they are coming under a different nursing situation, for one. They're doing -- they are then not -- it is also done for people that are, as I understand it, people that are going from one institution to another, a review is done there also.

Q: Is part of reason is because it's harder to monitor them when they're in restrictive housing?
A: I don't believe so.

Q: Okay. Is part of the reason that they might go a longer time before seeing medical staff in restrictive housing?
A: I don't believe so.

Q: You agree it's important to do daily nursing rounds in restrictive housing?
A: It's a standard practice a lot of the places, and often recommended. The importance of it would -- would depend on the amount of care needed. If -- if the inmates in a particular unit were all perfectly healthy, taking no medication and having no medical issues, then the daily round by the nurses would be actually a waste of time. But it's done anyway so that -- I assume that it's not missed in the situations where they need to give insulin regularly or medication three times a day. You check on the folks that need more checking, but it's not an absolute benefit to every inmate or even every unit.

Q: Well, I'm not asking you about the outcome. I'm just asking you, you agree, as a general matter, it's important to do daily nursing rounds in restrictive housing, correct? MS. SMITH: Objection; asked and answered.
A: As I said, in the overall, but it's not an absolutely that -- it's a benefit that a certain amount of it's overdone.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Is it recommended by the National Commission on Correctional Health Care?
A: I believe so.

Q: And why is it recommended? MS. SMITH: Objection; predicate.
A: The "whys" of that, you would have to ask the committee that wrote and approved that, what all they took into account.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. So is part of the reason why the daily nursing rounds are done is that because -- well, let me back up. If daily nursing rounds were not done in restrictive housing, would that increase the risk of medical harm to people in restrictive housing? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: I don't think that the issue was whether or not -- is whether or not there are daily rounds. It's that the appropriate care is provided for each inmate according to their need. If you could -- if you could devise a different method of having that in restrictive housing without a daily nursing round, I would be all for it, but as long as their needs are being met.
05_chunk_0018.title: 05 (chunk 19/61)

05_chunk_0019.text:
their need. If you could -- if you could devise a different method of having that in restrictive housing without a daily nursing round, I would be all for it, but as long as their needs are being met.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Well, right, again, and I am not asking about the outcome, I am asking about the risk. Does not doing the daily nursing rounds increase the risk of medical harm to people in restrictive housing? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad.
A: The risks are known and come to be known from outcomes. I'm sorry, they're not -- they're not -- they cannot be -- they cannot be divorced from each other. How do we know what a risk is unless we have known outcomes?

A: That is a risk factor --

Q: So --
A: -- because the blood pressure is poorly controlled. Well, controlled blood pressure has little effect.

Q: So somebody with persistently high and uncontrolled blood pressure has a high risk -- higher risk of having a heart attack even if they never have a heart attack, correct?
A: Correct.

Q: And so that's the same question I'm asking about the rounds, is if in general, does not doing those nursing rounds in restrictive housing increase the risk of medical harm in restrictive housing? MS. SMITH: Objection; overbroad; asked and answered.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Well, you're telling me about the prison system, right, and -- for example, the NCCHC says -- recommends to do the daily nursing rounds. Q: And they make that recommendation for a reason, right? MS. SMITH: Objection; predicate.
A: Yeah, I would assume so.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. And that reason is because, in general, if you don't do them, it increases the risk of medical harm to the -- MS. SMITH: Objection. THE COURT REPORTER: I'm sorry. MS. SMITH: Sorry. I didn't -- I thought you were finished, Dante. Did you get his question? THE COURT REPORTER: No. THE WITNESS: Yes, I did. MS. SMITH: Hold on one moment, Doctor. I was asking Kelly. SMITH: Objection; overbroad; asked and answered. Go ahead, Doctor.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. Let me ask you this in a slightly different direction. Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) I don't think you answered my question, Doctor. Did you form an opinion on whether the risk, the medical risk, to inmates in restrictive housing in Florida is higher than that in the general population? MS. SMITH: Same objection.

05_chunk_0019.title: 05 (chunk 20/61)

05_chunk_0020.text:
howed harm, either historically or within FDC, physical harm to people in restrictive housing of the sort that FDC does. So I would have to say I have no evidence to support that, that is higher risk.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) So did you form an opinion about the risk of harm? MS. SMITH: Objection; asked and answered; vague.
A: The same answer. I looked at the available evidence and arrived at -- and it was inadequate evidence of -- that would support the opinion of harm -- of increased risk of harm to restrictive housing inmates.

Q: (BY MR. TREVISANI) Okay. So it sounds like you did form an opinion, and you don't think that there was an increased risk; is that fair?

Q: We talked a little about the quality assurance you've done in Oregon. Would you agree that conducting quality assurance is important in a prison medical care system?
A: I think it's felt important in all medical care systems.

Q: Why is that?
A: The goal is -- is to maintain and, whenever possible, improve the quality of care.

Q: What sort of outcome should you look at when doing quality assurance?
A: That would depend a lot on your particular circumstances and history that, in my opinion, is best individualized. So we don't do outcome measures on how many of the inmates at OSP get annual mammograms over the age of 50 because there are no women at OSP with breasts.

Q: Okay. Should -- well, in your review of the information for this case, is Florida conducting quality assurance of the medical being provided in restrictive housing?
A: As a separate entity?

Q: No, just in general.
A: But as separate category, restrictive housing as a separate category? Is that your question?

Q: That's what I'm asking.
A: I'm not aware.

Q: Okay. Are they -- the same question but more (inaudible). Are they conducting quality assurance of the medical care being provided generally in Florida prisons?
A: Yeah, I understand that that is being done.

Q: Did you review any of those quality assurance be reports or documents?
A: I don't believe I got any of those, no.

Q: Do you think reviewing that is important when evaluating the medical system in prison?
A: It depends on what evaluations I was doing.

Q: Okay. For the work in forming your opinion in this case, do you think it would be important to review the quality assurance documents?
A: It was important to know that quality assurance was being done. It would be a little odd, I should think, from what I was asked to do, and I am doing, to redo their work, that is, looked over their shoulder at each of their assessments of each inmate's circumstances and outcome that they looked at for the quality assurance measures.
